newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks end New Year rally on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks end New Year rally on profit-taking.

text.p: Mexican stocks ended a run of record-breaking sessions on Monday as profit-taking finally set in.

"After a week-long rally dealers had to take profits. Nonetheless, we see no causes for concern unless the Dow Jones becomes volatile," said Rodolfo Campuzano, an equity analyst at the Invex brokerage.
"The bourse still has to extend its consolidation period to break through at (resistance of) 3,600 points," he added.
The leading IPC share index closed down 34.54 points, or 0.96 percent, at 3,561.55.
Dealers said profit-taking was most notable in blue chips that had led last week's run of five record closes in a row.

"Stocks that weigh heavily in the IPC, like Telmex, Televisa and Cemex, reached resistance last week. Some were jacked up more on Friday, so it was inevitable they would adjust and drag the market down," a desk trader from the Abaco brokerage said.
Telecommunications firm Telmex and media group Televisa fell 14 centavos (2 cents) and 3.70 pesos (47 cents), respectively, to 14.40 ($1.84) and 102.80 pesos ($13.13).
Cement firm Cemex CPO series meanwhile ended off 10 centavos at 31.05 pesos ($3.97).
Volume was 103.9 million shares traded, but dealers said two hefty cross trades accounted for at least one-third of the total.
On the broad market, 103 stocks changed hands, of which decliners outnumbered gainers by 45 to 35.
The most heavily traded stock at the head of the sliders' list was Simec, steelmaking arm of the debt-ridden Sidek group, which fell 9 centavos (1 cent) to 89 centavos (11 cents).
"Not much money ever steps into stocks like Simec, just day-trippers. If good stocks are cheap, why bother with the bad ones?" one trader said.
Traders said the gainers' list was headed by small unrepresentative trades.
"These stocks are not very marketable and their holding companies sometimes buy them to raise prices. There is nothing special in such price movements," one trader said.
